hints: Focus on which gas in air just sits there doing nothing at room temperature, even though it makes up 78% of air.
Remember that nitrogen exists as $\text{N}_2$ molecules with a very strong triple bond, $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$, with bond energy around 945 kJ mol$^{-1}$.
Link that huge bond energy to activation energy, the first bond that must be broken before any $\text{N}$ and $\text{O}$ atoms can combine.
walkthrough:
**Spot the real reactants**

Think side by side with me. Air is mostly $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$ molecules, not separate atoms. The reaction is:
$$\text{N}_2(\text{g}) + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow 2\text{NO}(\text{g})$$

**Ask which molecule is hard to break**

Oxygen reacts easily at normal temperatures, it supports combustion. Nitrogen does not. The key difference is bond strength.

**Compare the bond energies**

$\text{O}_2$ has a double bond, $\text{O}=\text{O}$, about 498 kJ mol$^{-1}$. $\text{N}_2$ has a triple bond, $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$, about 945 kJ mol$^{-1}$, almost twice as strong. That triple bond gives a very high activation energy.

**Explain the need for extreme heat**

Only a car engine or lightning provides enough energy to break the $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ bond and start the reaction. So the lack of reactivity of nitrogen due to the strength of the bond in $\text{N}_2$ is the main reason.

options.A: The half-filled 2p subshell ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$) does make a single nitrogen atom relatively stable, but the reactants here are $\text{N}_2$ molecules, not atoms. The inertness in air is due to the very strong $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond that must be broken, not the atomic electron configuration.
options.B: Correct and reassuring. $\text{N}_2$ is very unreactive because of its extremely strong triple bond. Breaking it needs a huge input of energy, giving a very high activation energy, so only very high temperatures allow formation of nitrogen oxides.
options.C: Oxygen is not the unreactive partner. $\text{O}_2$ reacts readily in combustion and respiration. Electron-electron repulsion in a paired 2p orbital does not make oxygen inert, and it is not the barrier to this reaction.
options.D: The $\text{O}=\text{O}$ double bond is much weaker than the $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond and $\text{O}_2$ is already quite reactive. Breaking $\text{O}_2$ is not the difficult step that demands lightning or engine temperatures.
